text: A function that builds a circuit and a function that runs it are two different responsibilities with two different reasons to change. Keeping them separate is the single architectural decision that makes everything else in this chapter — backend abstraction, multi-SDK support, testability — possible.

This lesson covers why mixing circuit construction and execution in one function creates hidden coupling, the dependency-injection pattern applied to quantum backends, how to refactor a does-everything function into construction, execution, and analysis, and what this separation unlocks later in this chapter.

Here's a common pattern in quantum tutorials and, unfortunately, a lot of real research code: one function that builds a Bell-pair circuit, instantiates a simulator, runs it, and returns the counts — all in one place. This function has three responsibilities glued together: it builds the circuit, it decides which backend to run on, and it decides how many shots to use, with no way to change any of them independently.

Three concrete costs follow directly. You cannot unit-test the circuit construction without actually instantiating and running a simulator, because the two are in the same function — every unit test secretly becomes an integration test. You cannot run this on a different backend without editing the function's source code every time. And you cannot reuse the circuit-building logic in a different context without copy-pasting the construction lines out.

The fix is dependency injection: the function receives the backend as a parameter, rather than reaching out and constructing it internally. Here, build_bell_pair does pure circuit construction with no backend at all, and run_circuit takes the circuit and backend as parameters, knowing nothing about what the circuit is for. Now the caller decides the backend, and a test can exercise build_bell_pair alone, with zero backend involvement.

When you encounter a function mixing construction and execution, split it using a four-step checklist: extract every line that builds the circuit into its own function; extract every line that executes it into a separate function taking the circuit and backend as parameters; make the backend a required parameter with no default pointing at a specific real backend; and write a construction test against the first function alone, with no backend import anywhere in that test file.

Next lesson formalizes exactly what kind of object that backend parameter should be — a shared interface that a simulator, a noisy simulator, and real hardware all implement identically, so algorithm code never needs to know which one it's talking to.
